hook: Passwords are slowly dying, and the thing replacing them is much harder to steal.

blocks.narration: Passwords are slowly dying, and the thing replacing them is much harder to steal. It is called a passkey.
blocks.visual: Sleek dark UI with a glowing old-fashioned password field cracking apart, neon accents

blocks.narration: With a password, a secret travels to the website every time you log in. If a fake site tricks you, it can steal it.
blocks.visual: A glowing string of characters flies from a phone toward a convincing fake login page

blocks.narration: Passkeys work completely differently. Your device creates two mathematically linked keys, one public and one private, using strong cryptography.
blocks.visual: Two glowing keys appear, one floating to a server, one locking into a phone

blocks.narration: The website only stores the public key. The private key never leaves your device, so there is nothing useful to leak.
blocks.visual: A server vault opens to show only a public key, while the phone keeps the private one hidden

blocks.narration: When you log in, your device proves it has the private key, usually after your face, fingerprint, or screen lock.
blocks.visual: A fingerprint glows on the phone and a green handshake line connects to the server

blocks.narration: Fake sites cannot use it, because passkeys are tied to the real website's address. Phishing simply has nothing to grab.
blocks.visual: A fake login page reaches for the key and finds an empty glass box

blocks.narration: Most major services now support passkeys, and they can sync across your devices through your password manager or account.
blocks.visual: Several devices glow in a row as a passkey icon syncs across them

blocks.narration: Turn on passkeys for your email account first, since it unlocks everything else. Follow for more tech that makes life easier.
blocks.visual: The phone glows softly with a shield icon as the camera pulls back

cta: Turn on passkeys for your email first. Follow for more tech that makes life easier.

captions.hook_line: Passwords are dying. Here's what replaces them and why it's safer 🔑
captions.body: Passkeys use a pair of cryptographic keys: the public key sits with the website and the private key stays on your device. Because there is no password to type, phishing sites have nothing to steal.

youtube_title: Passkeys Explained: Why Passwords Are Dying
